newsitem.title: INDIA: India must raise oil prices but with consensus - PM.
newsitem.headline: India must raise oil prices but with consensus - PM.

text.p: India will have to raise the prices of petroleum products to tackle a soaring oil pool deficit, Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral said on Thursday.

"There is no way out but to hike the prices of petroleum products," Gujral told state-owned Doordarshan television in an interview. "But we have to evolve a consensus. We cannot do it in a hurry. It does take some time."
Gujral said it was better that the issue of a rise in petroleum product prices was thoroughly discussed among the partners in the ruling centre-left coalition.
"It is not possible to buy these products at high prices and sell them at lower prices," Gujral said.

Last Sunday the ruling United Front's decision-making Steering Committee met to discuss measures needed to tackle the oil pool deficit but resistance by left-wing parties prevented from reaching consensus.
Left-wing parties in the United Front have opposed raising prices, instead favouring increasing crude oil production and cutting import duties on crude oil and petroleum products.
Front spokesman Jaipal Reddy said on Sunday that the government was unlikely to take a decision on the issue until the next committee meeting expected in 10 days' time.
"We are thinking of two or three alternatives (to deal with the oil pool deficit)," Gujral said. "We have to see what can be accepted and what cannot be accepted by people."
"We will also have to see what effect it will have on various items," he said.

Gujral said in both Bangladesh and Pakistan the prices of diesel oil and liquefied petroleum gas were much higher than in India. "The prices of petroleum products in India are almost half of the prices in Pakistan and Bangladesh," Gujral said.
Both Gujral and Finance Minister P. Chidambaram have said the government must soon decide how to repay money it owes to oil companies for selling petroleum products at well below global prices.
The outstanding amount, called the oil pool deficit, totalled 155 billion rupees ($4.33 billion) at the end of March 1997 and is expected to rise to 245 billion rupees by March 31, 1998.
Gujral said he would discuss the issue with the chief ministers of various Indian states and take their advice before taking a final decision on the issue.
